text: A key architectural difference publishers of GPT-4o, Claude, and Gemini all share is that they are:
options: Decision-tree ensembles optimized for tabular data
Purely retrieval systems with no generative component
Rule-based expert systems with hand-written logic
Transformer-based large language models trained on massive text (and often multimodal) corpora
explanation: GPT-4o, Claude, and Gemini are all transformer-based large language models trained on huge datasets; they differ in training data, fine-tuning approach, and multimodal capabilities, not in the underlying architecture family.

text: In the context of LLM APIs, a "token" is best described as:
options: Always exactly one character
A chunk of text (often a word, part of a word, or punctuation) that the model's tokenizer splits input/output into for processing
Always exactly one word
A unit of GPU compute time
explanation: Tokens are the units a model's tokenizer breaks text into — commonly whole words, sub-word pieces, or punctuation — and are the basis for both context window limits and API pricing. They don't map 1:1 to characters or words.

text: Why do most LLM providers price input tokens and output tokens differently?
options: It's arbitrary and has no cost basis
Generating (output) tokens is typically more computationally expensive per token than processing (input) tokens, so output is usually priced higher
Input tokens are always free
Output tokens are cheaper because they are cached automatically
explanation: Generating each output token requires a full forward pass and is inherently sequential, making it more compute-intensive per token than processing input in parallel — which is why output tokens are usually priced higher than input tokens.

text: What is the main benefit of using a streaming response from an LLM API instead of waiting for the full completion?
options: It reduces the total number of tokens generated
It guarantees a lower price per token
It automatically retries failed requests
Tokens are delivered incrementally as they're generated, letting the UI display output progressively and reducing perceived latency
explanation: Streaming sends tokens to the client as soon as they're generated rather than waiting for the entire response, which significantly improves perceived responsiveness for user-facing applications even though total generation time is unchanged.

text: Function calling (tool use) in an LLM API allows the model to:
options: Directly execute code on the provider's servers with no application involvement
Emit a structured request (function name + arguments) that the calling application recognizes and executes, then feeds the result back to the model
Permanently modify its own weights based on the function's output
Bypass the context window entirely for tool results
explanation: Function/tool calling lets the model output a structured call (matching a schema the developer defined) instead of prose; the application executes the actual function and returns the result to the model as additional context for its next response.

text: An embedding, in the context of LLM APIs, is:
options: A compressed version of the original text with characters removed
A cryptographic hash of the input used for caching
A dense numerical vector representation of text that captures semantic meaning, used for similarity comparisons
The system prompt encoded as base64
explanation: Embeddings map text (or other content) into a dense vector space such that semantically similar inputs produce vectors that are close together — enabling similarity search, clustering, and retrieval use cases.

text: A hard limit on the total tokens (input + output) a single request can use is called the model's:
options: Rate limit
Temperature ceiling
Context window
Token budget policy
explanation: The context window defines the maximum combined token count a single request can span; exceeding it causes the request to fail or forces truncation, independent of rate limits (which govern requests over time).

text: When would fine-tuning a model be preferred over retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for a given use case?
options: When the goal is to teach the model a consistent style, format, or specialized task behavior rather than to inject frequently changing factual knowledge
When the underlying facts change daily and must always be current
Fine-tuning is always strictly better than RAG in every scenario
When you want to avoid any upfront training cost
explanation: Fine-tuning is well suited to teaching consistent behavior, tone, or task-specific patterns baked into the model's weights. RAG is generally better for injecting current or frequently changing factual knowledge without retraining.

text: An API returns HTTP 429 with a rate-limit error. What is the recommended handling strategy?
options: Immediately retry in a tight loop as fast as possible
Implement exponential backoff with jitter before retrying
Give up permanently and stop the application
Switch to a different API key without any delay to bypass the limit
explanation: The standard, provider-recommended pattern for handling 429 rate-limit responses is exponential backoff with jitter — waiting progressively longer between retries with some randomness — rather than retrying immediately or hammering the endpoint.

text: Which factor is generally LEAST relevant when choosing which model to use for a production feature?
options: Latency and throughput requirements of the feature
Cost per token at expected usage volume
The color scheme of the provider's developer dashboard
The model's capability on the specific task (reasoning, coding, summarization, etc.)
explanation: Model selection should weigh task capability, latency/throughput needs, and cost at scale. Cosmetic details of a provider's dashboard UI have no bearing on the model's suitability for a production workload.

text: A "mini" or "nano" tier model (e.g. a smaller model in a provider's lineup) is typically chosen over the flagship model when:
options: The task is simpler or high-volume, and lower cost/latency matters more than squeezing out the absolute best quality
Maximum reasoning capability is required regardless of cost or latency
It is always strictly more capable than the flagship model
Function calling needs to be disabled
explanation: Smaller/cheaper model tiers trade some capability for significantly lower cost and latency, making them a good fit for simpler, high-volume, or latency-sensitive tasks where the flagship model's extra capability isn't needed.

text: What is a key practical advantage of open-source/open-weight models (e.g. Llama-family models) over closed API-only models?
options: They can be self-hosted, fine-tuned, and run offline without sending data to a third-party API
They are always more capable than every closed model
They require no compute resources to run
They automatically stay updated with no maintenance
explanation: Open-weight models can be downloaded, self-hosted, and fully fine-tuned, giving teams control over data residency, customization, and offline operation — trade-offs closed API-only models don't offer, in exchange for owning the infrastructure.

text: Why might an application send the same large system prompt or document on every request to an LLM API that supports prompt caching?
options: To let the provider reuse previously processed portions of the prompt, reducing latency and cost on repeated shared prefixes
Because caching is not possible with LLM APIs
Because it guarantees a completely different response each time
Because it disables rate limiting
explanation: Prompt caching lets providers skip reprocessing an identical prefix (like a long system prompt or reference document) across requests, cutting both latency and cost for the cached portion on subsequent calls that share it.

text: If a request repeatedly hits the model's context window limit when including conversation history, which is the most appropriate fix?
options: Ignore the error — it resolves itself over time
Increase the temperature parameter
Summarize or truncate older parts of the conversation history before sending, or switch to a model with a larger context window if appropriate
Switch to a smaller, cheaper model with less capability
explanation: The direct fix for exceeding context limits is to manage what's included in the request — summarizing/truncating older history, retrieving only relevant context, or moving to a model with a larger context window if that's the real constraint.

text: Multimodal LLM APIs (e.g. accepting images alongside text) typically bill image inputs by:
options: Never billing for images — they are always free
Charging only if the image contains recognizable text
A flat one-time fee regardless of how many images are used across all requests
Converting the image into an equivalent token count (often based on resolution/size) that counts toward the request's token usage
explanation: Most multimodal APIs convert image inputs into an equivalent token cost — often scaling with resolution or tile count — which is added to the request's token usage and billed alongside text tokens.
